title: 'Khali pet gold jita hai': Why India's kabaddi team did not eat before Asian Games final
text: Reuters Photo Indiaâs menâs kabaddi team had one thing on their mind before the Asian Games final - winning gold. So much so that the players did not eat properly before their title clash against Iran. âKhali pet gold jita hai,â captain Pawan Sehrawat said after India defeated Iran 40-34 to retain their Asian Games menâs kabaddi title on Saturday. Watch Anahat Singh on World Junior title, PV Sindhu, LA 2028 & her senior ambitions | TOISA Spotlight âThose 40 minutes were importantâ India had prepared well for the final, but Pawan knew the result would only be decided on the mat. âI was very excited about the match. I was very excited about what was going to happen in the match in the evening. Even if we know that we are playing well, we have practised well. But until the result comes, it stays in the mind. Those 40 minutes were important,â Pawan told IANS. India went into half-time trailing 17-18 but produced a strong second-half performance to turn the match around. Arjun Deshwal and Devank Dalal led the attack, while Sumit and Jaideep played important roles in defence. India turn the final around With 10 minutes left, India moved five points ahead after Arjun got past Iran captain Fazel Atrachali and helped India inflict an All-Out. Sumit then made an important tackle on Amirmohammad Zafar Danesh, while Rahul Sethpal also made a key defensive contribution late in the match. The win completed India's unbeaten campaign and gave them their ninth Asian Games gold medal in men's kabaddi. For Pawan, however, the wait for the result made the final even more emotional. âEveryone is emotional, so I get emotional at such moments. And it was that once the 40 minutes are over, we will eat and drink well. Not just one, but after that gold has come,â he said. Keeping an eye on Indiaâs medal tally Pawan also revealed that the players were following India's position on the medal table during the Games. âWe were seeing on the way that if our two golds are added, then where will we go? Till that time, as far as I could see, we were in sixth. And since then, we have not used the mobile properly. I don't know which number we will have in our medal tally,â he said. Because it is because of him that this medal has come to me,â he said. He also urged the government to consider Randhir for the Dronacharya Award, pointing out that several Arjuna Award winners had trained under him. âJapan has created history for meâ Pawan, who was one of Indiaâs flag-bearers at the opening ceremony alongside Manu Bhaker, also spoke about his experience in Japan. âJapan is very beautiful. For me, Japan has created history. I was a flag bearer. I was with such a good athlete, Manu Bhaker. For me, it is a miracle,â he said. title: Asian Games 2026: Why Indiaâs six-medal haul fails to improve ranking as China races towards 100 gold
text: L-R: Baranica Elangovan, Suruchi Singh, Kamaljeet and Gulveer Singh India enjoyed a six-medal haul on a packed Friday at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, but the surge was not enough to improve its position in the overall medal standings as the competition at the top intensified. India added one gold, two silver and three bronze medals to take its tally to 23 â two gold, nine silver and 12 bronze. Yet India remained 12th in the medal table after Day 6. The reason is simple: medal-table positions are primarily determined by gold-medal counts, and several countries ahead of India continued to add golds at a faster rate. Watch Shaili Singh opens up on long jump journey, injury struggles and personal best target Six medals but India remain 12th Indiaâs gold came from shooting, where Suruchi Singh and Kamaljeet combined to win the 10m air pistol mixed team title. Gulveer Singh claimed silver in the menâs 10,000m, while Indiaâs menâs 50m rifle 3-position team also finished second. Manpreet Kaur won bronze in the womenâs shot put, while table tennis pair Manush Shah and Diya Chitale also secured bronze. Baranica Elangovanâs historic bronze in womenâs pole vault completed Indiaâs six-medal haul. Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | Schedule Baranica became Indiaâs first-ever Asian Games medallist in pole vault across both the menâs and womenâs events. Despite the haul, India remained behind Kazakhstan, which had eight golds compared with Indiaâs two. South Korea occupied third place with 13 golds, while Japan had 28. China closing in on 100 gold medals At the top, China continued to pull away from the field, reaching 98 gold medals, along with 37 silver and 24 bronze, for a total of 159 medals. One of the biggest contributors to that dominance has been swimming, where China finished with 30 golds from 41 events. Teenage sensation Zhang Zhanshuo played a major role in that haul, becoming the first swimmer to win seven gold medals at a single Asian Games. The 19-year-old won the 400m freestyle in 3:41.28 on Friday, adding to titles in the 200m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle as well as three relay golds. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines His seven-gold haul surpassed the previous Asian Games swimming benchmark of six golds, set by Chinaâs Zhang Yufei at Hangzhou 2022 and Japanâs Rikako Ikee at Jakarta 2018. Only North Korean shooter So Gil San, with seven golds and a silver at the 1982 New Delhi Games, has won more medals at a single Asian Games. Chinaâs dominance was not confined to swimming, with the country continuing to collect gold medals across disciplines. Its 98 golds leave it just two short of the landmark 100-gold mark, while Japan is a distant second with 28. title: Neeru Dhanda: From tin cans and a borrowed gun to World Cup history and Asian Games gold
text: Indiaâs Neeru Dhanda celebrates after helping the womenâs trap team win silver at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya. Dhanda also qualified for the individual final after finishing joint-second in qualification with a score of 118/125. From being inspired by her cousin Lakhsay Sheronâs Asian Games medal to winning one herself, Neeru Dhanda has completed a remarkable journey - and in the process, created a piece of history for Indian shooting. The 26-year-old Indian shooter produced a stunning 28/30 in the womenâs trap final to clinch gold at the Asian Games on Tuesday. Chinaâs Sun Yunong finished second with 26, while Kuwaitâs Hajar Abdulmalik took bronze with 21. Dhandaâs 28 also shattered the previous Asian record of 24. The Indian had already announced her intent by topping qualification with 118 hits out of 125, and she carried that form into the six-shooter final to produce the biggest result of her career in the process delivering India its first individual gold medal of the 2026 Games and taking the countryâs tally to five gold medals and 47 overall. Watch One Point Cost Him Asiad Selection in 2018. 8 Years Later, Ahvar Rizvi Is Back | TOISA Spotlight Earlier in the day, Dhanda had already played a central role in Indiaâs womenâs trap team silver, joining Aashima Ahlawat and Manisha Keer to finish second behind China. For Dhanda, the triumph comes just months after she broke new ground at the ISSF World Cup in Lonato, Italy. In July, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold medal in trap at an ISSF World Cup. Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | Schedule The Asian Games gold now gives that World Cup success a continental dimension. Dhanda had arrived in Aichi-Nagoya as the reigning Asian champion, having won gold at the 2025 Asian Shooting Championships. She also had a mixed-team bronze from the ISSF World Cup in Almaty earlier this year. From tin cans to the Indian Army and World Cup glory Dhanda was inspired to take up shooting after watching her maternal cousin Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Lakshay Sheoran win a silver medal in men's trap at the 2018 Asian Games. Sheoran also lent her his gun when she was beginning her journey in the sport. Years later, Dhanda has followed him to the Asian Games podium, but has gone one better by winning gold. The rise has been backed by the Indian Army, where Dhanda serves as a Naib Subedar in the Corps of Military Police. She trains at the Army Marksmanship Unit in Mhow and works with foreign coach Peter Wilson, the London 2012 Olympic trap champion. title: Asian Games 2026: Full India athletes list, sport-wise squads and events
text: PV Sindhu, Mirabai Chanu and Lovlina Borgohain (Agency Image) The Asian Games 2026 will bring together athletes from across the continent in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, with the event scheduled from September 19 to October 4. A total of 45 countries and regions are set to compete across 43 sports. India will enter the continental event after a record medal haul at Hangzhou 2023, where the country collected 107 medals, including 28 gold, 38 silver and 41 bronze. The Indian contingent will feature five individual Olympic medallists despite Neeraj Chopra withdrawing from the Games following an ankle injury. PV Sindhu, Manu Bhaker, Lovlina Borgohain, Aman Sehrawat and Mirabai Chanu are among the prominent names in the squad. Cricket will see India defend both its men's and women's titles. Shreyas Iyer will captain the men's T20 side, which includes teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, while Harmanpreet Kaur will lead the women's team. Hockey will also carry significant importance because the men's and women's competitions will double up as continental qualification events for the LA 2028 Olympics. title: Meet Suchika Tariyal, the 36-year-old who had 'given up' on her sporting career and is now India's first MMA Asian Games Medalist
text: Photo: @KirenRijiju/ X There are moments in a sportspersonâs career that are important simply because of what their score says; then there are those whose backstory of hope is worth listening to. One such deeply inspiring story is about Suchika Tariyal's bronze medal at the Asian Games 2026. On the very first day of the Games, the 36-year-old stepped into a sport making its Asian Games debut and clinched a piece of history for India, defeating a Mongolian participant 2-0 in the quarterfinals of the women's traditional 60kg mixed martial arts category. Meet Suchika Tariyal, who bounced back stronger at 36 after hitting rock bottom and won a silver for India at the Asian Games 2026 Suchika Tariyal has given India a historic moment at the Asian Games 2026. On Day 1 of the competition, the 36-year-old secured a bronze medal in mixed martial arts by defeating Mongolia's Altanchimeg Baigalmaa 2-0 in the quarterfinals of the women's traditional 60kg category, which is also MMA's very first appearance at the Asian Games, held this year in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. What makes this win particularly interesting is the tumultuous road that led here. Tariyal was not an MMA fighter at all; she was a judo player for years, representing India at the 2022 Commonwealth Games and later at the 2023 Asian Games in kurash, in a traditional form of jacket wrestling. Later, a knee injury, along with a tough stretch in her personal life, pushed her away from the sport she had loved. At one point, she had essentially decided to walk away from competitive sport altogether. How did she come back to her sporting journey? It took two people from India's MMA circle to change that. UFC fighter Pooja Tomar and former ONE Championship fighter Himanshu Kaushik convinced her to give the sport another shot. "I had given up. I thought, 'Alright, it's fine, it's done, this is enough,'" Tariyal said, according to Hindustan Times. "Then Pooja and Himanshu forced me to try it once, saying that my skills were good and I would pick it up quickly. These two are the ones who brought me into MMA," she added. Her way to Asian Games 2026 was full of ups and downs. She had been a Jiu-Jitsu World Champion in 2024 and was preparing along that path, but in January, the jiu-jitsu team for the 2026 Asian Games was dropped, and the format changed, suddenly ending the path she'd been training for. She came back stronger, this time trying out for MMA, and her decision has now paid off with a medal. Tariyal was harassed as a child Tariyal has also spoken about a difficult childhood experience that influenced her early relationship with trusting people. She recalled being harassed while getting a haircut as a child, which left a lasting mark. "As a child, you don't understand what is happening. I went into depression, and I developed a hatred towards men," she said, according to Hindustan Times. That mistrust, she has said, lasted well into adulthood, until she met her husband, Kapil, whom she married in her thirties. "I got married in my 30s, only after meeting Kapil, because I had never met a man like him before," she said. She added that her mother had once doubted whether she would ever marry at all, given how deeply she distrusted men. Of Kapil, she said, "His trust in me makes me feel that if I had gotten all this support earlier, I could have done even better. " Looking for trusted parenting advice? title: Asian Games 2026: India one step away from defending kabaddi gold medals as men and women storm into finals
text: India's Men and Women's team reach final of the Asian Games 2026 (Agency Images) Indiaâs kabaddi team continued their dominance at the Asian Games 2026 as both the menâs and womenâs teams secured their places in the gold-medal matches with semifinal victories. The womenâs side defeated Nepal 48-24, while the menâs team followed with an emphatic 66-27 win over Thailand. The results ensured that India will have a chance to defend both kabaddi titles at the Aichi-Nagoya Games. For the women, the victory kept alive their bid for a fourth consecutive Asian Games gold medal. India have won the womenâs kabaddi title at every Asian Games since the sport was introduced to the womenâs programme in 2010. India women overpower Nepal The Indian women established control early and went into the interval with a 31-17 advantage. India combined successful raids with a disciplined defensive effort and repeatedly put Nepal under pressure. The four all-outs in the opening half gave the defending champions a substantial cushion. Nepal struggled to match India's intensity after the break. They managed only seven points in the second half as India maintained their advantage and eventually completed a 24-point victory. The win extended India's unbeaten run in the competition. They had previously defeated Iran, Bangladesh and Japan during the group stage. The defending champions will now turn their attention to the final, where they will look to maintain their remarkable record in the women's event. Men produce another dominant performance The men's team delivered an equally commanding performance against Thailand. India raced into an early lead and were comfortably ahead at 37-18 at half-time. Thailand showed flashes of resistance, with Theeradat Chaisit producing a strong spell in attack, but India quickly regained control. The Indian side continued to pile on the points after the break and eventually crossed the 50-point mark. Thailand could not keep pace with India's raiders and defenders as the gap continued to widen. India eventually closed out the semifinal with a 66-27 victory. title: Jay Meena battled typhoid, hip injury and self-doubt to win historic Asian Games medal
text: Indian athlete Jay Meena, winner of the Bronze Medal in soft tennis at the Asian Games 2026, arrives at the IGI Airport, in New Delhi on Thursday. (ANI Photo/Neeraj) NEW DELHI: Weeks before the 2026 Asian Games , Jay Meena was bedridden with typhoid and a severe infection, losing eight kilograms in the process. Sent home to Dewas in Madhya Pradesh from an Asian Games training camp in Srinagar in August, the 25-year-old needed his parents to feed him by hand for nearly a week. Recovery was difficult too. For a week, he would feel dizzy after walking just a few steps. An iffy stomach only made his attempts to regain his strength and return to shape more challenging. Watch Shaili Singh opens up on long jump journey, injury struggles and personal best target Cut to the present. The moment his opponentâs final shot drifted long and Meena won Indiaâs first-ever Asian Games medal in Soft Tennis, the 25-year-old collapsed onto the baseline in joy. Moments later, he was back on his feet, arms spread wide and roaring towards the Indian bench. The celebration marked far more than a bronze medal. It was a historic moment for Indian Soft Tennis, with Meena securing the countryâs first-ever Asian Games medal in the sport. Meena narrates that for 15 days, he was completely out of action and the clock on the Asian Games was ticking down. All his efforts over the course of the past few months had just been undone by the viral infection. âI started light warm-ups, I started training again. I could not sit at home at such a moment,â he tells TimesofIndia.com, with the urgency of the situation still quite evident in his voice. He recovered just in time to board the flight to Tokyo and the Shinkansen (train) to Nagoya. The ordeal, however, was far from over. New Delhi, Sep 24 (ANI): Indian athlete Jay Meena, winner of the Bronze Medal in soft tennis at the Asian Games 2026, receives a warm welcome from his family members and supporters on his arrival at the IGI airport, in New Delhi on Thursday. (ANI Photo/Neeraj) Recovering from typhoid meant nutrition became almost as important as training. But in Nagoya, the predominantly seafood menu offered few vegetarian options. In the absence of a traditional Games village, he made do with corn, bread, butter, milk and cereal. While urging the authorities to send a chef alongside future contingents, Meena stressed that pre-packaged foods cannot replace fresh preparations. The lingering effects of the illness surfaced during his semi-final loss to Japanâs Takuya Kurosaka (2-4), as Meena required a medical timeout to continue the closely contested match at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Center. He later revealed that a hip niggle was preventing him from playing his backhand, with a âpinchingâ pain each time he went for the shot. Then there is the obvious mental challenge of representing the country at such a competition. Little by little, the chances of winning a medal got smaller and the internal battles got bigger. First, the menâs team, also featuring Meena, lost 0-2 to Indonesia in the quarter-finals. Then, Meena and Aadhya Tiwari lost in the first round of mixed doubles. âThere were a lot of disappointing nights, a lot of self-doubts that we had all night. When we lost the quarter-final against Indonesia, it was a big opportunity on the 18th. If we had won that day, then Soft Tennis would have opened the (medal) account for India. After that, there was (the) mixed doubles in which Aadhya and I reached the pre-quarter-finals but lost. So, there were very disappointing nights going on day by day,â said Meena in reflection of the start of the competition. âAfter all these things, it was very difficult to come back and gain confidence after the self-doubt. It was very difficult to wake up every morning with new hope and get on the court with a new zeal,â he continued. Nagoya: Indiaï¿½s Aadhya Tiwari and Jay Meena compete in the mixed doubles group B soft tennis match in the ongoing 20th Asian Games, at Higashiyama Park Tennis Center , in Nagoya, Japan. (PTI Photo/Arun Sharma)(PTI09_21_2026_000029B) A career that almost wasn't and brother's sacrifice The desperate need for belief and confidence is not new to Meenaâs career. When he was in Class 10 and his foray into Soft Tennis was not going anywhere, Rameshwar, his lawyer father, suggested stepping away and focusing elsewhere. It was then that his mother stepped in and pushed for a rethink and patience. That punt paid off. Years later, Meena began rewriting Indian Soft Tennis history, winning National Games gold, Indiaâs first World Championships medal in mixed doubles, and a breakthrough Asian Championships bronze. Still one of his biggest supporters, Meenaâs father travelled with his son to national tournaments and even accompanied him to Japan for the Asian Games. The financial condition was not so good. We had to force him to stay back because my father could not afford more than what was costing me to play. Thatâs why my brother went into Engineering. Jay Meena The hardest sacrifice, perhaps, belongs to someone else: his younger brother Yash. Two years younger than Jay, Yash was a Soft Tennis player and national medallist. But with their financial condition less than ideal, a hard decision was needed and Jayâs career continued. âThe financial condition was not so good. We had to force him to stay back because my father could not afford more than what was costing me to play. Thatâs why he went into Engineering,â says the MP native. âSomewhere or the other, my younger brotherâs life was sacrificed because of me. Because my parents paid more attention to me for about 10 years. If we had continued, then maybe he would have been with me in the Asian Games,â he continued. From gully cricket to Soft Tennis courts Jay Meena was like many other youngsters in the country who harboured cricket ambitions. He would play gully cricket with other kids in his street. The notorious boy in him, though, tended to pick up fights and get into altercations. Even at school, he would bother the teachers, including once setting off fireworks under his principalâs desk. The situation came to a head when he was rusticated from Ebenazer Higher Secondary School in the fourth grade. With no school willing to take him in, Pioneer Public School agreed, but on one condition: that he join the sports academy. With his parents keen on keeping Jayâs antics in check, they agreed to sports coach Sudesh Sangteâs condition. ** TO GO WITH STORY** Nagoya: India's bronze medalist Jay Meena, front right, poses on the podium with gold medalist Toshiki Uematsu, top left, of Japan, silver medalist Takuya Kurosaka, front left, of Japan, and bronze medalist Chen Po-yi, top right, of Chinese Taipei during the medal presentation ceremony for the soft tennis men's singles event at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026, in Nagoya, Japan. (PTI Photo)   (PTI09_25_2026_000201B) Sangte, a former national-level Kho Kho player and now the national Soft Tennis coach, had set up a two-court facility. âMy family was very upset with me. I would not stay at home, I would not allow anyone to relax. I used to fight. Their parents used to complain a lot and my family threw me out. They said, you are out now. You stay on the ground [academy]. Donât come home in the morning and evening. Come home at night,â Jay says with a laugh. âThe school teachers and my classmates were (also) upset. I was rusticated in the fourth grade. And no other school was admitting me. At that time, Mr. Sudesh Sangte, who is my head coach now, he got me admitted. I took admission during the summer holidays.â âThey had made two courts in their school. So, I was playing in their academy during the summer holidays. I didnât even know, when I started playing for India and now won the Asian Games medal,â he explained. For me, this is an Olympic medal. Itâs no less than an Olympic medal. All the strongest teams come in the Asian contingent. So this feels like an Olympic medal to me because Soft Tennis is not part of the Olympics Jay Meena Bigger than an Asian Games medal Even though the International Soft Tennis Federation (ISTF) has 65 members, including Eritrea, Basque Country, Curacao, Malta, North Korea and Uganda, the sport is dominated by Asian countries. At the last World Soft Tennis Championships, held in Anseong, South Korea, in 2024, six countries had picked up medals: Korea, Japan, Chinese Taipei, China, India and the Philippines. In the end, athletes from Japan, Chinese Taipei, North Korea, South Korea, Indonesia, India and the Philippines walked away with medals. Considering the dominance of Asian countries in Soft Tennis, Jay weighs this new medal on an Olympic scale. âFor me, this is an Olympic medal. Itâs no less than an Olympic medal. All the strongest teams come in the Asian contingent. So this feels like an Olympic medal to me because Soft Tennis is not part of the Olympics,â the youngster explained. title: Meet Zhang Zhanshuo: The 19-year-old who won seven golds at the Asian Games; from a kid who âcouldnât swimâ to a Chinese swimming star
text: His gold medals came in the men's 200m, 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, along with three relay titles. At six, Zhang Zhanshuo was the youngest swimmer in a local competition and had barely begun learning the sport. At 19, he left the Asian Games 2026 with seven gold medals and a place in the record books. The Chinese swimmer became the first swimmer to win seven gold medals at a single Asian Games when he won the men's 400m freestyle at the Aichi-Nagoya Games on September 25. His seven golds also equalled the Asian Games record for the most individual gold medals won at a single edition, a mark that had stood for 44 years. He competed in eight events and won seven of them. His gold medals came in the men's 200m, 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, along with three relay titles. His 200m freestyle victory also produced an Asian record, while his 400m and 800m wins came in Games-record times. But Zhang's relationship with swimming began for a much simpler reason. âA seaside kidâ who had to learn to swim Zhang started learning when he was around five and a half to six years old. Zhang was born in Qingdao in May 2007. His mother had been a middle-distance runner for the Shandong provincial team, while his father had also competed in athletics when he was younger, according to reports from Chinese media Qingdao. His father, Zhang Xunshan, has recalled that the original idea was not to turn his son into a professional swimmer. They lived in a coastal city, and he felt that a child growing up by the sea should at least know how to swim. Zhang started learning when he was around five and a half to six years old. As reported by Qingdao News, he trained for about half a year before entering the 2013 Qingdao primary and secondary school swimming competition. He was below the minimum age for the competition, but that did not stop him from taking part. The result surprised everyone. The six-year-old Zhang, the youngest competitor at the event, won six gold and two silver medals. At that stage, there was little indication that the boy would eventually become one of China's leading swimmers. A year later, Zhang was selected by Qingdao swimming coach Liu Ziqian and began systematic training with the city team. Liu later recalled that Zhang was the youngest swimmer in the group, training alongside athletes who were three or four years older. His family came from sport Zhang's parents understood the demands of competitive sport themselves. His mother had competed in middle-distance running for the Shandong provincial team, while his father had been involved in athletics. That background also helped his first coach recognise his physical potential. âWhen I took over, Zhang Zhanshuo was just over seven years old,â Liu told Qingdao Daily. âThis child had talent from a young age because his mother had been a middle-distance runner for the Shandong team, and his father had also been an athlete when he was young. â Zhang's rise was gradual after that. He began making a name for himself at provincial competitions before breaking through on the national stage as a teenager.By 16, he had won two gold medals at the 2023 Chinese National Swimming Championships. In 2024, he was part of China's world-championship-winning 4x200m freestyle relay team. The swimmer who keeps coming from behind One of Zhang's defining moments came during the men's 4x200m freestyle relay at the 2026 Asian Games. China was behind Japan going into the final leg. Zhang took over the anchor position and gradually closed the gap before overtaking Japan in the final stretch. His split was 1:42.92, and China finished in 7:00.17, breaking the Asian record. After the race, Zhang was asked about the dramatic comeback. His answer was short: âNormal, normal. â His teammate Pan Zhanle had a very different way of describing what had just happened. Pan, who had previously been Zhang's childhood hero and was his teammate in the relay, called him a âmiracle childâ after the race. Seven golds and a new record After touching the wall, Zhang sat on the lane line and counted his medals on his fingers. â1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7!â Zhang's biggest moment came four days later. On September 25, he won the men's 400m freestyle, setting a Games record and securing his seventh gold medal of the competition. After touching the wall, Zhang sat on the lane line and counted his medals on his fingers. â1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7!â âJust after I got out of the water, I counted my gold medals from one to seven. I wanted to express that I had won seven gold medals,â he told the media. His seven golds equalled the record for the most individual gold medals won at a single Asian Games. The previous record had belonged to North Korean shooter So Gil-san, who won seven golds at the 1982 New Delhi Games. Zhang also became the Chinese athlete with the most gold medals at a single Asian Games. He still gave himself '85 out of 100' Despite the seven gold medals, Zhang did not describe his Asian Games campaign as perfect. As reported by Xinhua, he gave himself a score of 85 out of 100 and said he still had technical areas to improve, particularly his turns. Zhang said after the Games: âOne step short of perfect.â He also made it clear that the seven medals were not where he wanted the story to end. âThe Asian Games is not the goal. I'm still aiming for the Olympics and competing with the best,â Zhang said, according to the South China Morning Post. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Trouble in Japan! Indian athletes face accommodation, food and transport woes ahead of Asian Games 2026
text: Nagoya: Commuters walk past a banner ahead of the 20th Asian Games at the railway station in Nagoya, Japan. (PTI Photo/Atul Yadav) NAGOYA: Torrential rains battered this city last week, forcing evacuations, disrupting train services and even prompting the rescheduling of some Asian Games events. Step into Nagoya today, though, and there is little sign any of it ever happened. As the city braces for the possibility of Typhoon Dujuan hitting the Aichi-Nagoya coast on Monday next, another storm has been brewing around the organising committee. Sustainability and cost-cutting may have been at the heart of the decision to do away with a traditional Games village, but the arrangement has instead triggered chaos and confusion for hundreds of athletes and officials. Watch Japanâs Asian Games Mess: India, China Athletes Left High & Dry On Arrival I Cost-Cutting Chaos For many of the 17,000 athletes and officials arriving in the city, the wait at the airport to get their credentials validated and transport arranged has been at least three hours, with some stranded for as long as 14 hours. Already weary from their journey, they were left waiting at the airport, with food and basic arrangements becoming an issue. The problems, which began earlier in the week, continued on Thursday, two days before the Games officially open on Saturday. The confusion did not end at the airport. Athletes arriving at their accommodation were faced with uncertainty over room allocation, with even the hosts caught up in the mess. A section of the Japanese contingent had to seek alternative arrangements after men and women were allotted shared rooms. Indian Olympic Association officials too faced room-allocation issues and were left without accommodation before alternative arrangements were eventually made. Space has emerged as another concern. While compact accommodation is hardly unfamiliar in Japan, the cramped quarters have taken several contingents by surprise. The Costa Serena cruise ship, docked at Kinjo Pier, is housing around 4,000 athletes. Japanâs deputy chef de mission Hisashi Mizutori acknowledged the problems at a press conference on Thursday. âSince the cruise ship village opened, athletes have been arriving and going through the entry procedures. However, the process took a significant amount of time due to issues with activation of their credentials,â he said. The container-style huts, built with an eye on future use as disaster evacuation facilities, have also come under scrutiny. âThere is no space to store luggage and we are not here for few days but three weeks, so itâs a challenge in the containers. The ones built for acclimatisation back home by Sports Authority of India were much bigger,â rued an IOA official, an Asian Games veteran. Food has been another source of discontent. While some contingents found fare difficult to adapt, others complained that quantities were inadequate and were forced to eat outside. Travel woes for shooters Logistical problems continued to hit contingents on Thursday. With venues spread across the region and accommodation located some distance away, athletes have been spending hours on the road and, in some cases, missing scheduled training slots. The Indian shooting team was among those affected. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The journey from their accommodation to the Aichi Prefectural General Shooting Gallery was expected to take around 75 minutes. Instead, the team took more than two hours to reach the venue after waiting nearly three hours for transport to arrive. By then, the Indians had missed their allotted practice slot and had to wait for other teams to finish before getting their turn. Away from the chaos, Nagoya is preparing to welcome the Asian Games back to Japan after a 32-year gap. The industrial and automotive hub is decked out in Games posters and buntings, with trains, subways and streets carrying the colours of the event. Amid the organisational troubles, locals have stepped up. title: First gold for India at Asian Games 2026: Harmanpreet Kaur-led women's cricket team beats Sri Lanka in final
text: Team India wins Asian Games Gold. (Pic credit: BCCI Women) NEW DELHI: Harmanpreet Kaur-led side opened India's gold medal account at the Asian Games 2026 on Tuesday, defeating Sri Lanka in the women's cricket final at Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin to end the country's wait for a top-podium finish in Aichi-Nagoya. The defending champions produced a dominant performance in the gold-medal clash, first posting a mammoth 216/3 after opting to bat before bowling out Sri Lanka for just 69 to seal a commanding 147-run victory. The result gave India their first gold and seventh medal overall at the Asian Games , with the tally now standing at one gold, four silver and two bronze medals. Watch Jyothi Yarraji opens up on injury comeback, Asian Games qualification & 12.5 Target Smriti Mandhana, Shafali Verma and Richa Ghosh were the architects of India's imposing total. Mandhana smashed 79 off 45 balls, while Shafali contributed 48 off 29. Richa then provided a spectacular finish, remaining unbeaten on 49 off just 22 balls. India's batters cleared the boundary 13 times during their innings as they posted their highest-ever total in women's cricket at the Asian Games. Mandhana and Shafali gave India a flying start, adding 99 for the opening wicket before the latter was dismissed for her brisk 48. Mandhana continued her assault and brought up her half-century before eventually falling for 79. Harmanpreet made 19, but Richa ensured there was no let-up in India's scoring rate. Her unbeaten cameo, which included six fours and three sixes, took India past the 200-run mark and set Sri Lanka a daunting target. With the ball, India maintained their dominance. Deepti Sharma (3/6) took three wickets, while fellow spinners Shafali Verma (2/3), Shreyanka Patil (2/9) and Shree Charani (2/13) claimed two wickets each as Sri Lanka were bowled out for a modest total. India join Pakistan with two Asian Games cricket golds The triumph means India now have two women's cricket gold medals at the Asian Games, having also won the women's cricket gold for the country in 2023. India had not participated when cricket featured at the Asian Games in 2010 and 2014. Their 2023 title and Tuesday's triumph now put them level with Pakistan, who won the women's cricket gold medals in 2010 and 2014. The men's competition will begin later in the Games, with the Shreyas Iyer-led Indian side scheduled to start their campaign in the second quarterfinal on September 28. India are also the defending men's Asian Games champions. On Day 2, Himanshu Dhillon won silver and Rudrankksh Patil bronze in the men's 10m air rifle individual event. Dhillon finished second behind China's Olympic champion Sheng Lihao, who successfully defended his Asian Games title with 254.2 points, while Patil secured bronze with 230.9. Dhillon and Patil then combined with Parth Mane to claim another silver in the men's 10m air rifle team event, taking India's shooting haul to five medals. India's other Day 2 medal came from Suchika Tariyal, who made history by becoming the country's first Asian Games medallist in mixed martial arts. She was awarded bronze after her semifinal against Singapore's Hui Hoon Teo ended in a draw, with Teo advancing under the competition's tie-break rule after Suchika was around 700 grams heavier at the morning weigh-in. title: Asian Games 2026: Go for gold! Saurav Ghosal identifies India's biggest challenge, and incentive
text: Anahat Singh carries India's gold medal hopes in squash at the 2026 Asian Games. (ANI) New Delhi: For the first time in 24 years, Saurav Ghosal will watch an Asian Games from the sidelines. The former India No. 1, whose first appearance in the continental event came in Busan 2002, stepped away after nine medals: two gold, two silver and five bronze. But he did so with one lingering regret: no singles gold medal. Now, his role has changed. Ghosal is a mentor to teenage sensation Anahat Singh, who carries India's gold medal hopes to Aichi-Nagoya. With squash also offering direct qualification to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics for its gold medallists, the stakes are higher than ever. Watch Saurav Ghosal on Indiaâs Asian Games squash hopes, Anahat Singh and Olympic qualification In a conversation with TimesofIndia.com, Ghosal reflected on watching instead of playing, preparing Anahat for the biggest tournament of her young career, and why India should judge this squad by medals â not merely potential. "I wish I was there. I wish I was still playing. Kind of the best times of your life, of my life at least," Ghosal said of missing his first Asian Games since 2002. For Ghosal, the Asian Games always stood apart from the professional tour -- not because of the attention it attracts, but because of what it represents. "It's more to kind of have the honour to play for India, win for India and be proud doing that. I think that kind of makes it internally something which is bigger than a normal event," he admitted. I wish I was there. I wish I was still playing. Kind of the best times of your life, of my life at least Saurav Ghosal is not at the Asian Games for the first time since 2002 The straight knockout format, he added, leaves little room for error. "You kind of need to be laser-focused at these events because one bad day can destroy the entire event. Especially in a sport like ours where it's straight knockouts. So you focus on yourself, focus on the things that you need to do well. And you focus on both what you do on court and off court. That's equally important in an event where it's quite long as well, which is different to what we do on the professional tour. I think all those things are things that you focus on more rather than things that can happen outside of your bubble," he explained. Anahat's gold medal preparations: Clarity over change File photo of India squash player Anahat Singh. (PTI) Eighteen-year-old Anahat Singh enters the Games after a remarkable rise that has made her one of India's genuine medal contenders. Rather than altering her game, Ghosal says the focus has been on tactical clarity against specific opponents. "She's a well-rounded player overall. I think it's about understanding who you're playing in this event, what your opposition is going to look like, trying to get extreme clarity on how you're going to play them, how you respond to what they're going to do to you and do so in a manner that works in your favour," said 40-year-old Ghosal. Execution, he believes, is the difference between preparation and performance. "There is no guarantee that it will work out. But you have to put the building blocks in place in your mind to be able to have a chance to produce it on court," he reasoned. Anahat arrives carrying expectations few Indian teenagers have faced in squash. Ghosal's advice is rooted in the mindset that sustained him throughout his own career. Saurav Ghosal alongside Anahat Singh. "The good thing about her is that she's quite carefree. She's a happy-go-lucky person. So that helps. I think that's helped her through the years. The expectations go back to the same thing that it's not in your control. And it's all about perception," said Ghosal. "When I was playing, I always thought that if there was expectation, that means people actually believed in me. And that means I had something about me (that) I was actually good enough. It was almost like a re-emphasis of the belief that I had in myself that, 'OK, I might actually be good enough to do this.'" The key, he says, is preventing the mind from drifting towards outcomes. "If you just think of it on those lines when you're playing, it's a bit like fooling your mind a little bit with all the necessary information there is to kind of occupy it so that you don't have time to think about, 'Oh, what if I don't win a medal?' Because that is not going to help you win. That is not going to help you play better." You almost crowd your mind with all the things that you need to do to play well. And it's almost like the antithesis of an idle mind is a devil's workshop Saurav Ghosal "So you almost crowd your mind with all the things that you need to do to play well. And it's almost like the antithesis of an idle mind is a devil's workshop. "So you don't want that mind to be idle in a negative way. You want that mind to be calm, but you still want things to be going on in your mind which are related to you playing better. And that's things that you do on court, but also off court. It's helped me over the years and that's what we're telling Anahat to do as well," he added. Genuine contenders and an Olympic opportunity Former India coach Major Maniam has labelled both Anahat and Abhay Singh as genuine medal hopes, a view Ghosal shares. "There's no doubt that both of them come into these Games as genuine medal contenders. It would be disappointing for them personally if they didn't win a medal at least." The bigger prize, however, is gold. Under the qualification system, the Asian Games singles champion earns a direct place at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where squash will make its Olympic debut. Ghosal acknowledges that the Olympic incentive makes the tournament "definitely bigger" but insists it isn't a daily talking point within the camp. "It would be disappointing for them personally if they didn't win a medal at least. Obviously, the big prize at these Asian Games is the gold because that gives you the Olympic qualification spot. And that obviously is the big one. And it's hard and rightfully so. Getting an Olympic qualification spot shouldn't come easy. "The idea obviously is that whether Anahat wins this or doesn't win it, she is going to gun for the Olympics. And when you get to the Olympics, you want to try and win something. So it's a journey that has to happen. Even if she wins the gold here and gets in the Olympics, it doesn't stop there because that doesn't guarantee you anything. It guarantees you being there, but you're not going to be there just to make up the numbers. You're going to be there to try and do something. So I think that journey continues," added Saurav. title: 'My life is complete now': Mirabai Chanu ends 12-year wait for Asian Games medal
text: Mirabai Chanu (PTI Photo) Mirabai Chanu finally has the Asian Games medal she had been chasing for 12 years. The Indian weightlifter won silver in the women's 49kg category in Japan on Wednesday, lifting a total of 198kg (87kg+110kg). It was India's first Asian Games weightlifting medal since Karnam Malleswari won silver in 1998. Chanu had already won an Olympic silver in Tokyo in 2021. Her return to Japan five years later gave her the chance to complete her collection of major medals. Watch Anahat Singh on World Junior title, PV Sindhu, LA 2028 & her senior ambitions | TOISA Spotlight "Finally, I have got the medal that I wanted, which I have been chasing for 12 years. I am feeling very light now because the pressure is completely gone from me. This is my dream Asian Games medal. I feel my life is complete now," Chanu said after her event. The 32-year-old said she had been waiting for this moment since she started competing at the Olympics. "I won a silver medal in Tokyo (Olympics) and now I have a silver medal at the Asian Games in Japan. I've been dreaming of winning an Asian Games medal since I stepped into the Olympics. "I always ask myself, what is happening to me during or before every Asian Games? But this time, I tried my best. I came here with the resolve that no matter what happens, I will win the medal," added the 32-year-old. 'Everything is special' for Chanu Chanu said the Asian Games medal is as important to her as an Olympic medal because many of the world's top weightlifters are from Asia. Asked what made Wednesday special, Chanu pointed to several things. "Everything is special. Olympic rings, hairband, nails." Chanu also wanted to finish the competition knowing that she had given her best. She attempted 111kg in the clean and jerk even though she could have won silver with a lower weight. "I wanted to lift more than 110kg (in clean and jerk). I didn't know how much the Indonesian (bronze medallist) would lift. I knew the gold is not there for me. But I just wanted to give my best performance. I didn't want to win a medal by lifting less. Chanu yet to decide on 53kg category The 49kg category will not be part of the 2028 Olympics, with the 53kg category set to replace it. Chanu said she has not yet taken a final decision on when she will begin preparing for the new weight category. "We have not decided finally, but we will try. Qualifying starts from December but we have not yet decided whether we will start or not (from December). But for now, I will enjoy." Chanu also explained why moving up to 53kg will require careful planning. "I have been playing in 49kg. When I am in training, I maintain 1.5kg more, say 50.5kg. Maintaining that is difficult for us. I have to do weight training. I have to take a lot of load. That's it. "For now, there will be no problem. LA will start from 53kg. In will be my last 49kg. So, on one hand, it is very good." Weight gain will come with strength Chanu said she does not want to increase her body weight quickly. Her focus will be on building strength and muscle along with gradually increasing her weight. "If we gain weight suddenly, our performance can also go down. Strength will also not be that much. We are thinking of increasing the weight along with strength. "To bring more strength to the muscles, we will maintain it (weight). I will keep track of what I want to eat, what I want to change in my diet. If I get 53kg at once, my strength can go down. So, I have to control my weight along with my strength." "After the Commonwealth Games, I had very little time. At that time, I had to control my weight in 48kg. It was very difficult for me to control and maintain my weight. "It was very important for me to maintain my weight in 49 kg. But the Asian Games were very important for me. I had been preparing for this for years. So, I have maintained everything." title: 'Final mein gai, to gold hi layegi': Suruchi Inder Singh's coach after Asian Games 2026 triumph
text: Suruchi and her teammate Kamaljeet won gold in the 10m air pistol mixed team event (Image credit: Agencies) NEW DELHI: âFinal mein gayi, to gold hi layegi,â an elated Suresh Singh said after his student Suruchi Inder Singh helped India win its first gold medal of the day at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Friday. Suruchi and her teammate Kamaljeet won gold in the 10m air pistol mixed team event, finishing on top at the Aichi General Shooting Range to give India its second gold medal of the Games. For Suruchi, the victory came after a disappointing individual event. Watch Anahat Singh on World Junior title, PV Sindhu, LA 2028 & her senior ambitions | TOISA Spotlight The Haryana shooter, who won four individual World Cup gold medals in 2025 in Buenos Aires, Munich, Lima and Doha, including the World Cup Final, failed to qualify for the final in the individual 10m air pistol event. In a field of 55 shooters, she finished 26th in qualification with a score of 568-12x. âShe was disappointed. But I knew she would come back stronger. She knows how to bounce back quickly, and that is her best quality. The moment she reached the final, I was 200 percent sure that she would win gold. Thatâs how she is,â the coach said. Suruchi's gold-winning show Suruchi and Kamaljeet were in control from the start of the mixed team final. The pair scored 103.0 in the first series of Stage 1, followed by 202.4 and 303.5. They continued their strong performance in Stage 2, scoring 364.7 in the first series and staying comfortably ahead of South Korea and Iran. After 18 shots, India remained at the top and extended their lead with a score of 424.9 in the second series of Stage 2. Suruchi and Kamaljeet eventually finished with a total score of 484.6 to win the gold medal. South Korea's Suhyeon Hong and Gaeun Choo finished second with 478.0. The Korean pair were 6.6 points behind the Indians, underlining India's control of the final. âShe is an athlete for the finals. Look at her past record. If she has reached the final, then you can't stop her. She will go for gold. She doesn't want silver or bronze. She has that kind of hunger,â Suresh said. Hours of work before the Asian Games Ahead of the Asian Games, Suruchi worked on several aspects of her shooting with Suresh at his Guru Dronacharya Shooting Academy in Bhiwani. The coach said they focused on her technique, holding and dry-fire training. Suruchi's father had initially wanted her to take up wrestling. âShe worked on her holding and did dry-fire training for hours to improve her focus. We also worked on some technical aspects,â he said. title: At 12, she was eve-teased, it changed her life; 24 years later, Suchika Tariyal is Indiaâs first Asian Games MMA medallist
text: Suchika Tariyal NEW DELHI: At 12, an incident of eve-teasing changed the course of Suchika Tariyalâs life. What began as a need to protect herself eventually became a journey through judo, Ju-Jitsu and mixed martial arts. And on Sunday, the 36-year-old Rohtak native broke new ground for Indian MMA at the Asian Games . Tariyal defeated Mongoliaâs Altanchimeg Baigalmaa 2-0 in the womenâs traditional -60kg quarterfinal at the Aichi-Nagoya Games to enter the semifinals and guarantee India at least a bronze medal. Watch Vishal TK: 'Asian Games my only focus after record-breaking yearâ In the process, she became the countryâs first athlete to secure an Asian Games medal in MMA, which is making its debut at the Games. From self-defence to a life in combat sports The decision to take up judo after the eve-teasing incident was never meant to lead to a career on the international stage. But Tariyal steadily turned herself into one of Indiaâs most versatile combat athletes. She began with judo before moving to Ju-Jitsu and eventually MMA in 2017. Her judo career brought eight national titles and international success, including gold at the 2019 Commonwealth Judo Championships and the 2019 South Asian Games. She also won silver at the 2018 Commonwealth Judo Championships and competed at multiple Asian championships. Suchika Tariyal (@suchika_tariyal Instagram) At the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, she competed in the womenâs -57kg category and narrowly missed a medal. Her transition to Ju-Jitsu produced another major achievement when she won gold in the adults Ju-Jitsu Contact Female -63kg category at the 2024 JJIF Ju-Jitsu World Championships. Tariyal made her MMA debut with a victory in 2017 but took a seven-year break from the sport while continuing her judo and Ju-Jitsu career. She returned to professional MMA in December 2024 after signing with BRAVE Combat Federation and won at BRAVE CF 92 in Bahrain. âJudo set me up for MMA, which for me is the ultimate level of combat sports. Because of judo, I was skilful in ground fighting and grappling. I only had to learn the standing game and striking skills for MMA. Switching from judo was not difficult. MMA is a test of all-round skills, and one has to be a complete combat athlete,â she said. Second Asian Games, different story The Aichi-Nagoya Games represent a second chance for Tariyal. At Hangzhou in 2022, she competed in kurash, but the campaign did not produce the result she wanted. âLife has given me a second chance at the Asian Games. In Hangzhou, it did not go the way I wanted because kurash was not popular in India and my preparation was not adequate. This time, I am fully prepared for MMA,â Suchika told SAI Media. Supported by the sports ministryâs Target Asian Games Group (TAGG) scheme, she entered Aichi-Nagoya after winning back-to-back bronze medals at the Asian MMA Championships in January and May this year. Her rise has also made her a familiar face beyond the combat-sports arena. She has more than 300,000 Instagram followers and has featured on MTV Roadies and Prime Videoâs Indiaâs Ultimate Warrior. She has also been honoured by the President and Prime Minister for her international achievements and contribution to womenâs empowerment. But for Tariyal, perhaps the biggest purpose of her journey is what it can mean to young women. âI really want to inspire young women to take up MMA. I will be very happy even if one girl looks at me and says, âIf Suchika can, I can too.â In modern times, women need to defend themselves, and parents must let their children take up combat sports. MMA gives you that complete package. And women have a strong mindset to play combat sports. They can bear pain and can be more focused. If a woman can bear the pain of childbirth, MMA is nothing,â she said. title: Roshibina Devi wins silver, falls short against China's Zhang Xiaoyu in  Asian Games final
text: India's Naorem Roshibina Devi (PTI Photo) Indian wushu player Naorem Roshibina Devi secured her second consecutive Asian Games silver medal after losing the women's sanda 60kg final 0-2 to China's Zhang Xiaoyu at Aichi-Nagoya on Thursday. Zhang dominated the title clash, winning both rounds 5-0 to take the gold medal. She had lost the Hangzhou final to China's Xiaowei Wu. Roshibina enjoyed an impressive campaign in Japan, with her run including a victory over Vietnam's 2023 world champion Nguyen Thi Thu Thuy. title: Asian Games: India win womenâs team squash bronze after Anahat Singhâs heartbreak
text: India's Anahat Singh (ANI Photo) NEW DELHI: India added another squash medal to their impressive Asian Games 2026 haul as the womenâs team settled for bronze after a hard-fought 1-2 semifinal defeat to Hong Kong on Thursday. The result took Indiaâs squash medal tally at the Aichi-Nagoya Games to four, with Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh having earlier won silver medals in the singles events, while Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar had claimed bronze in mixed doubles. Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | Schedule Anahatâs missed chances prove costly A lot rested on 18-year-old Anahat in the opening match against Hong Kongâs Sin Yuk Chan. The world No. 17 Indian appeared in control after winning the first two games 11-9, 11-8, but the contest dramatically slipped away from her. Anahat led 10-6 in the fourth game and had four match points, but could not close out the match. Chan fought back to win the game 13-11 before taking the deciding game 12-10 to complete a 3-2 victory. Anahat had also recovered from a 7-9 deficit in the fifth game to level it at 9-9. Chan earned the first match point, which Anahat saved with a backhand drop, but the Hong Kong player remained composed, earned another match point and converted it to put Hong Kong 1-0 ahead. Tanvi keeps India alive, Joshna falls short With India facing elimination, Tanvi Khanna produced an excellent fightback against Ka Yi Lee. The Indian lost the opening game 4-11 but gradually found her rhythm, extending rallies and forcing Lee into errors. Tanvi edged a tense second game 13-11 after saving opportunities and then fought back from 3-7 down in the third to win it 11-9. title: Why was the Asian Games 2026 flag-hoisting ceremony delayed?
text: The Indian national flag among those of participating nations at the venue during the official welcome and flag-hoisting ceremony ahead of the 20th Asian Games, in Nagoya, Japan. (PTI Photo/Arun Sharma) NAGOYA: The clock is ticking for Japan, most unusually. A country synonymous with punctuality and quiet efficiency has been struggling with the clock in its role as Asian Games host. On Friday, the flag-hoisting ceremony for six contingents â India, Yemen, North Korea, Palestine, Chinese Taipei and Timor-Leste â was delayed by more than an hour because of what organisers described as âmiscommunicationâ between the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) and the Games organising committee (ANAGOC). Watch Devajit Saikia on Ajit Agarkar's future, IPL window & BCCIâs big AGM decisions The ceremony at Garden Pier was scheduled for 1:30 pm local time but was initially pushed back by 20 minutes, following which the ceremonial band began playing. However, just before the contingents were due to take the stage, they were asked not to proceed and were made to wait before eventually being sent back to the waiting area. No Indian athlete was in attendance, but chef de mission Sahdev Yadav and deputy chefs de mission Sharath Kamal, Anjali Bhagwat, Lijo Thottan and Alaknanda Ashok were present. Initially, the delay was attributed to the late arrival of the chief guest. An ANAGOC official later offered a different explanation. âThe communication between the Olympic Council of Asia executive board and the organising committee was not well, thatâs why this happened. Itâs not like somebody delayed the ceremony,â the official said. title: At 19, Pincky Balhara lost three family members ahead of Asian Games debut; Now, she is only Indian to win multiple Kurash medals
text: Bronze medalists Pincky Balhara of India (AP Photo) Three family deaths in quick succession could have brought Pincky Balharaâs sporting journey to a halt. Instead, the Delhi athlete carried her grief into the competition arena, turned her fatherâs dream into motivation and went on to win an Asian Games medal. Eight years after her historic silver at the 2018 Jakarta Asian Games, Balhara returned to the continental podium on Monday, winning bronze in the womenâs -78kg Kurash event at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Games. The bronze is Balharaâs second Asian Games medal in Kurash, following her silver in the womenâs -52kg category in Jakarta. She has now become the only Indian athlete to win multiple Asian Games medals in Kurash. Watch One Point Cost Him Asiad Selection in 2018. 8 Years Later, Ahvar Rizvi Is Back | TOISA Spotlight What is Kurash? Kurash is a traditional Central Asian martial art that originated in the region and is particularly associated with Uzbekistan. It made its Asian Games debut at the 2018 Jakarta Games. The basic objective is simple: throw the opponent onto their back while remaining in a standing position. Unlike judo or Brazilian jiu-jitsu, Kurash does not involve prolonged ground fighting. From judo mats to Kurash Born on October 20, 1998, in Neb Sarai, Delhi, Balhara began training in judo when she was nine. Her maternal uncle, Samundar Tokas, a former judoka and coach, played a major role in her early development. She quickly established herself in judo, winning gold at the 2018 Asian Junior Judo Championships. But she missed out on India's judo squad for the 2018 Jakarta Asian Games. That disappointment opened another door. With Kurash making its Asian Games debut in Jakarta, Balhara entered the trials. The sport, which shares similarities with judo but is contested entirely from a standing position, offered her another route to the continental stage. She made the team and was soon heading to Jakarta. Three deaths changed everything But just weeks before the Games, Balhara's life was shattered. She lost her cousin brother first, followed by her father, who died of a heart attack, and then her grandfather. The three deaths came in quick succession, leaving the teenager struggling to cope with the loss. Her father had been particularly excited about her selection for the Asian Games. After his death, Balhara initially did not want to compete. Her uncle, however, pushed her to continue, reminding her of her father's hopes for her career. She returned to training while dealing with grief and also had to make the weight for her 52kg category. She later recalled going to the gym at night because she feared people would judge her for returning to training so soon after her father's death. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Balhara eventually made it to the 2018 Asian Games and produced a remarkable run. At just 19, she reached the women's -52kg Kurash final, becoming one of India's first Asian Games medallists in the sport. She eventually lost to Uzbekistan's Gulnor Sulaymanova and settled for silver. Balhara later recalled her father's prediction before the Games: that she would win silver rather than gold. When she finished second, she remembered his words. At Aichi-Nagoya, Balhara began her campaign with a 3-0 quarterfinal victory over South Korea's Garam Lim, securing her place in the semifinals and guaranteeing India another Kurash medal. She then faced South Korea's Sumin Mo in the last four. Mo won 5-0, sending Balhara into the bronze-medal position. Eight years after her first Asian Games medal, Balhara was back on the podium.
